extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientists and graduate students interested in the nature of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and concepts for identifying, characterizing, and assessing 'normal science', paradigms, and scientific revolutions — i.e., how to judge when a body of research functions as a paradigm and when a revolution has occurred. Useful for historians, philosophers, and reviewers assessing the structure and development of scientific fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of normal science
rubrics_metrics.description: 'normal science' means research firmly based upon one or more past scientific achievements, achievements that some particular scientific community acknowledges for a time as supplying the foundation for its further practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal science is normally transmitted via textbooks that 'expound the body of accepted theory, illustrate many or all of its successful applications, and these applications with exemplary observations and compare experiments.' It presupposes shared commitments and standards among practitioners and is the prerequisite for focused, paradigm-based research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm: unprecedented and open-ended achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: A paradigm's achievement is 'sufficiently unprecedented to attract an enduring group of adherents' and 'sufficiently open-ended to leave all sorts of problems for the redefined group of practitioners to resolve.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigms include law, theory, application, and instrumentation together and serve as concrete models from which coherent research traditions spring (examples: 'Ptolemaic', 'Copernican', 'Newtonian', 'wave optics'). The dual requirement (novelty + problem-generating capacity) is central to judging whether an achievement functions as a paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific revolution: anomaly-driven extraordinary investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific revolutions begin when the profession 'can no longer evade anomalies that subvert the existing tradition of scientific practice' and 'begin the extraordinary investigations that lead the profession at last to a new set of commitments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revolutions are 'tradition-shattering complements to the tradition-bound activity of normal science.' Historically recognizable revolutions 'necessitated the community’s rejection of one time-honored scientific theory in favor of another incompatible with it' (examples: Copernicus, Newton, Lavoisier, Einstein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction of prior theory and re-evaluation of prior fact
rubrics_metrics.description: A new theory's assimilation 'requires the reconstruction of prior theory and the re-evaluation of prior fact, an intrinsically revolutionary process that is seldom completed by a single man and never overnight.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of a new paradigm often forces reinterpretation of previously gathered facts and may change what counts as admissible phenomena; reviewers should expect reinterpretive work accompanying paradigm shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery transforms both fact and theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific fact and theory 'are not categorically separable' and 'the unexpected discovery is not simply factual in its import' — discoveries can qualitatively transform the scientist’s world as well as quantitatively enrich it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: discovery of oxygen or X‑rays does more than add items to inventory; it prompts re-evaluation of procedures, entities, and the theoretical network. Assessment should account for such qualitative transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms direct problem selection and experimental focus
rubrics_metrics.description: A paradigm 'suggested which experiments would be worth performing and which, because directed to secondary or to overly complex manifestations, would not.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigm-based research is highly directed: it focuses fact collection, motivates design of special apparatus, and encourages more precise, esoteric work. Evaluators should judge research in light of the problems a paradigm makes salient.

rubrics_metrics.name: A theory need not explain all facts to be a paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: To be accepted as a paradigm, 'a theory must seem better than its competitors, but it need not, and in fact never does, explain all the facts with which it can be confronted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: Franklin’s fluid theory of electricity did not account for every repulsive effect but nonetheless became a paradigm because it unified many phenomena and guided productive research. Reviewers should not dismiss candidate paradigms for incompleteness alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm acceptance reshapes the professional community
rubrics_metrics.description: Reception of a paradigm can 'transform a group previously interested merely in the study of nature into a profession' through 'the formation of specialized journals, the foundation of specialists’ societies, and the claim for a special place in the curriculum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of a field’s maturity or professionalization should consider institutional changes that follow paradigm adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquisition of a paradigm signals field maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'acquisition of a paradigm and of the more esoteric type of research it permits is a sign of maturity in the development of any given scientific field.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mature fields exhibit shared paradigms, highly directed research agendas, and specialized communication; this is a criterion for evaluating developmental stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-paradigm stage: competing schools and random fact-gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of a paradigm, 'all of the facts that could possibly pertain to the development of a given science are likely to seem equally relevant' and 'early fact-gathering is a far more nearly random activity than the one familiar.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such stages produce multiple competing schools, ad hoc explanations, and morasses (e.g., Baconian natural histories). Reviewers should recognize that lack of coherence in early stages is typical and not necessarily evidence of poor scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm narrows the field and excludes dissenters
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'new paradigm implies a new and more rigid definition of the field. Those unwilling or unable to accommodate their work to it must proceed in isolation or attach themselves to some other group.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissenters are often marginalized or 'read out of the profession' (examples: astrology, romantic chemistry). Evaluators should note institutional exclusion as a sign of paradigm consolidation, but also examine marginalized work for possible overlooked insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm-induced specialization and esoteric communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a paradigm is taken for granted, research reports 'will usually appear as brief articles addressed only to professional colleagues' rather than books intended for general audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks leave foundational justification to be assumed; advanced work becomes narrowly targeted and less accessible. Peer review should take into account assumed background knowledge and the intended specialist audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition between scientific communities effects theory change
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Competition between segments of the scientific community is the only historical process that ever actually results in the rejection of one previously accepted theory or in the adoption of another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section XII treats the process replacing simple confirmation/falsification; reviewers should consider institutional and communal competition as mechanisms of change, not only logical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook tradition obscures revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbook tradition contributes to why 'scientific revolutions have previously been so difficult to see.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because textbooks present consolidated paradigms and leave out the contestatory processes, historians and reviewers must look beyond textbooks to controversies and anomalies to understand revolutionary change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of technology and crafts in early fact collection
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of paradigms, 'technology has often played a vital role in the emergence of new sciences' because crafts provide recondite data not casually discoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of early stages of a field should weigh contributions from technological practices and crafts (e.g., metallurgy, medicine) as legitimate sources of facts that later feed paradigm formation.
